definition: Invective means a sharp, angry verbal attack; harsh, insulting language.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word invective. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know invective should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The coach was fined after unleashing a stream of invective at the officials' table.
An insult is weaker than invective: an insult is a single cutting remark, while invective is a sustained stream of them.
Vitriol is stronger than invective — vitriol suggests language so corrosively bitter it burns like acid, while invective can be loud and abusive without that concentrated cruelty.

Abuse is the broadest word for insulting, degrading language, in any register — one muttered slur already counts. Invective is abuse at full rhetorical flood: a sustained, often loud and elaborate stream of insults delivered as an attack. A single ugly name is abuse; ten unbroken minutes of it is invective.

Denunciation means fierce public condemnation — it formally accuses its target of wrongdoing and calls on others to judge. Invective needs no charge at all: it is the harsh, insulting language itself, attacking the person rather than making a case against them.

Eighteenth-century London printers grew rich on political quarrels, and none paid better than the pamphlet war of 1768.
What began as a dispute over a rigged election spent exactly one page on the evidence.
After that, both sides abandoned argument for invective.
Week after week, fresh pamphlets poured out comparing the rival candidates to swamp rats, pickpockets, and plague — sustained, inventive name-calling with no charge left in it, only venom.
Readers stopped following the case entirely; they bought each new pamphlet the way one buys tickets to a fight.
